utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few preliminary matters first. The Prosecution would seek to recall Dr. Baccard to give further evidence in relation to the bodies of the women found in the well. We forecast that the evidence he could give in direct evidence would only take about ten minutes. His evidence will fit with other evidence going to show where the women came from but will be the only evidence going to show the manner in which they died and would go to show that they were alive when they were thrown into the well and would go to show, to some extent, in respect to two bodies that were capable of examination in sufficient detail, either that they very probably had been or may have been sexually assaulted before being thrown into the well to die. So it's important evidence, and it won't take very long to give, and in our respectful submission, the doctor could properly be allowed to give that evidence before he leaves, which he has to today, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we had an indication that you may make this application. We understand the importance of the evidence, but nonetheless, we are applying strict rules, strict rules to the length of time which the accused can have and strict rules to you as timing, and part of that procedure must be that we move along with the witnesses. To allow this witness to be recalled on a matter which should have been prepared beforehand and should have been part of his witness statement will take up the best part of an hour, I suspect. It's also evidence which, as far as I can see, has not been disclosed before, although I may be wrong about that. Nonetheless, we are going to apply strict rules to you as we apply them to everybody else. We understand it may cause inconvenience, but nonetheless, the Prosecution must be ready before it calls its evidence, like anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidence has in fact been disclosed in advance. The precise history of the oversight whereby the evidence was omitted the first time is not something I can deal with immediately. The Prosecution, I think, must make its position clear now, as it will have to in subsequent discussions about timing, that we will respectfully say that there has to come a time when the mere interests of the time of the case must be balanced against the interest of having the full evidence before the Chamber. We will do all that we can, as we have been from first to last, to deal with this matter expeditiously, but we would respectfully say that there will inevitably be occasions when things don't go perfectly, and we would invite the Chamber not always to say that such imperfections should lead to the exclusion of evidence. The second point I wish to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, let me deal with that since you make the point. The interests of time are not mere interests. They are in the interests of justice and the interests of justice are that this case is finished expeditiously. Secondly, of course there are occasions when the interests of time must give way to other considerations, and the Trial Chamber is fully alert to that. We will consider any applications you have in due course to call other evidence, but it must be made plain that this case is to be finished on time, and that means that the parties, both parties, must put on their case with the maximum of expedition. Yes. The next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next point relates to expedition, a topic, of course, to which I know we're returning generally next week, I think. K5, who is a witness in waiting and one that, for example, we may be able to take tomorrow if the other two witnesses were, happily, to be finished by then, is one in respect of whom the Chamber has made no order about adducing his evidence under 92 bis. I think the Chamber indicated on an earlier occasion it was provisionally not minded to grant the 92 bis application, subject to further discussion and argument; and in the interests of economy, may I just explain why the Chamber might think it appropriate to take his evidence under the provisions of 92 bis without necessarily ruling on the matter immediately, although we would need to have his statement subject to the 92 bis provisions today, which would involve our negotiating with the Registry about it. Would Your Honour just give me one minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are the reasons why 92 bis provisions might be appropriate: The time constraints, to which we've already made allusions; the fact that his evidence goes to acts and conduct of people other than the accused; and then as to the body of his testimony, the Chamber will recall that his testimony covers acts of arson, grenade attacks that he was obliged to engage in and aware of performed against the Albanian community one way and another. Now, that evidence, although of course it's important evidence, is nevertheless corroborative of the allegations of destruction of property, intimidation, and targeting of high profile Kosovo Albanians that has been given in general and specific terms by other witnesses. So those are the reasons why the Chamber might think that it is an appropriate witness for the provisions of 92 bis, but, Your Honour, that's as far as I'm going to go in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient to raise something in private session. Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the issue of 92, whether he's appropriate for 92 bis, it may be sensible if we confer for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered this. This is an exceptional witness in the nature of the evidence which he gives, which is unlike any other evidence we've heard. Given the background and the nature of the evidence, we think it should be given in full and not in statement form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will prepare accordingly. I'm grateful for that ruling. I was in error when I said that he was not being granted voice distortion. In fact your order of the 22nd of March permitted both facial and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, the next witness I'm going to be calling, Baton Haxhiu, it has been raised with me the possibility of reversing the order of witnesses. Mr. Ryneveld's dealing with that. I'll ask Ms. Graham just to go out and make sure it's going to be Baton Haxhiu next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Actually, if we could stick to that because too much variation makes it very difficult for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather he's in the witness room. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just on K5. It may help the proceedings if both parties agree that the Court has the statement of the witness in full. It might make it easier to navigate through his evidence, which is -- the statement is so detailed that I can foresee there will be problems without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we have that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've had it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we've got a revised summary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this connection with the next witness -- what's his name? Baton Haxhiu, yes. I think that it is quite clear that, according to your rules, he could not testify according to Rule 92 bis because he mentions and says in his statement -- talks about his statement -- in his statement about his alleged contacts with me, with the chief of security and so on and so forth. So he can't come under Rule 92 bis. He must give an entire, complete statement and testimony. And my second remark is: Why was this witness known as Witness K28 up until now? And why have these double listings for the witnesses both as secret and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him about that if you want. That's not a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to say, as I had indeed forecast yesterday, that there is one paragraph in the addendum to the statement which I'll take you to which would fall outside the potential for 92 bis procedure, and if the Court has the addendum, it's under the: "I would add the following: I first met Mr. Milosevic ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't received that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you haven't received that. It was dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the proposal is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That paragraph to be given in live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a press conference where ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing, please, that I wish to say. I don't mind what you're going to decide, I just wish to draw your attention once again to the violation of the Rules, because this is an additional statement, and as Mr. Nice said a moment ago and it was provided to me last night, after the end of business yesterday, and statements must be provided at least a certain amount of time before they are read. That is one point. Secondly, I was given all the material in English once again although we have a Trial Chamber ruling that I must be supplied with the documents in my own language. The other side has English as their mother tongue so I am receiving documents in the mother tongue of the opposite side, and that is a fine illustration on the small issue of the equality of arms of the two sides. That is to say that I am being provided with the material in the mother tongue of the opposite side let alone all the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's hear what the Prosecution have to say about this. When was this second statement? I see it's dated the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the addendum was only done yesterday in the process of preparation in the usual way where witnesses are taken through the material. These are matters he had to add. When we introduced the 92 bis procedure that we've been adopting with considerable judicial economy some weeks ago, it was on the basis that there might be occasional additional points to be made or corrections to be made, and as I understand it, although I haven't been in court for these witnesses, broadly similar practice have applied and there is nothing at all unfair in him adding -- in his adding to his previous statement by these one or two additional matters. The accused can no doubt deal with them. As to the English language version, we understand that the B/C/S translation will be with us shortly. We had a language assistant working on it all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say the translated version is now available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And might I, I hope without inconveniencing you, just add this point: To allow this additional material to be given, one way or another, is no different from what happens with witnesses who give evidence in full viva voce but whose proofing summaries add material exactly of this kind to their pre-existing statements in a way that's inevitable when witnesses come to the moment of giving evidence and are focused on the relevant history. Applying the 92 bis provisions to an addendum of this kind is simply a sensible use of our procedures to achieve judicial economy. We would, of course, be content, subject to the restrictions of time, simply to take addendums in full viva voce but there's no need to, in our respectful submission, in a case like this. Although the passage involving the accused directly should be given directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue really is whether the accused should have more time to prepare for cross-examination on this material. The answer may be to allow the evidence to be called and then, if the accused wants more time for cross-examination, we would have to consider that as a matter of fairness since he's not had time to prepare for this. Mr. Milosevic, we'll hear the witness, and you could cross-examine on the other statement. If you want to ask for more time to prepare for cross-examination on this one, then you shall -- we will consider that application if you think there's some matter which you need some time for preparation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you straight away I'm not asking for anything and I don't need more time. It's all the same to me. I'm just drawing attention to daily violation of the Rules that occur here in this room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three? One, two, three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt it was the volume on my controls.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have it now, thank you. You're not asking for more time. Very well. Your comment about the daily violation of the Rules is, of course, wholly wrong and inappropriate. We'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. 5 THE WITNESS: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the short evidence in chief from this witness in a couple of minutes' time. Before I do so, can I remind the Chamber that by his two statements, to which we will refer later, the witness gives an account of his having been involved in the founding of the newspaper Koha Ditore, and indeed he is a journalist in due course to receive an award in the United States of America at the 9th Annual Press Freedom Awards ceremony where he was awarded for his commitment to the defence of press freedom in Kosovo and throughout the world. His statements cover matters of which we've already heard in part, and sometimes substantially, including the history of the education problems and the education agreement in Kosovo, the non-violent demonstrations by students and others that led to protests in October 1998, which involved violent police intervention, and in the judgement of the witness, reaction thereafter by Albanians. He can speak, of course, of the violence perpetrated at the offices of the newspaper where he worked, of his own arrest and interrogation, and of the processes of negotiation between Kosovo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Albanians, including the person we've seen as a witness, Bakalli, and others that followed. He can deal with the meetings involving, amongst others, the man Stanisic, and indeed he's a witness who observed the participation in events by the last witness but one before this Tribunal, the witness Tanic. He can explain how the Serbian delegation at those negotiations indicated its implacable opposition to certain proposals and can remind the Chamber of the Burnt or Scorched Earth policy that was referred to by the Serbian side. He will be able to remind the Chamber of how it was that authority for negotiation appeared to be vested in and only in ultimately the accused and the man Stanisic who attended at a second meeting in December of which the witness can speak, in the course of which Stanisic said that the chief of police in Kosovo, Sreten Lukic, had convinced the accused to break up the students' peaceful demonstration by use of force, Stanisic saying that he could not decide anything on his own, although being emphatic that the proposition for a republic in Kosovo would never be accepted to those nationalistic circles surrounding the accused who were prepared to go to war. He, as a witness, expresses the view that the KLA was the product of Serb repression, of an inert international policy and, it may be, of the conservatism in the approach of President Rugova, again a witness from whom you've heard. This witness is one who, with no involvement on his own part or on the part of his family, lost five members of his family on his father's side, including a 9-year-old boy, in the course of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that summary, your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: My name is Baton Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement ought to be admitted, the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I was going to turn to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Haxhiu, sign declarations as to the accuracy of two statements that you have made?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first being a statement prepared at interview on the 20th, 21st, and 22nd of August of the year 2001, and the second being an addendum prepared as recently as yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. The first was taken down in Prishtina on the said date, the second yesterday. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second makes one or two corrections and amplifications, deals with the significance you see in certain documents, and deals with one face-to-face encounter you had with the accused. Turning to that, were you, as a journalist, present at a press conference in Ljubljana, Slovenia, in the late spring or early summer of 1990?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. It was in March or April of 1990. It was a news conference organised after the meeting held by the six presidents of the former republics of the former Yugoslavia, and I was there in the capacity of a journalist, represented then the newspaper Epoka. And I asked two questions of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The questions and his replies, if you please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Since I had read the book written by the accused where, on page 146, he had said that all issues are open issues, from the border to the kindergartens and the creches, then taking my queue from that statement, I asked the accused: "When are you, Mr. Milosevic, going to get rid of chauvinism and enable the Albanians of Kosovo to determine their own status and win the status of the Republic of Kosova?" And he answered, "This will never occur because the Albanians there are in minority and they don't have the right to self-determination and we are not going to allow secessionism in Kosova and do everything we can to prevent that from happening."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say there were two questions you asked. Was the other one of any significance?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please switch the microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. Yes. The book to which the witness refers has been located in the building. The passage to which he refers has been translated. They're both being brought to court pretty well immediately. And, Your Honour, with your leave, I would just ask two other questions arising from the supplementary material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In addition to the book to which you've referred, do you regard one or two other documents of particular significance, documents that were published at that time? If the answer to that is yes, can you, but very shortly, in a sentence or so, explain what the documents were and their significance, they being documents that you know we don't have here in the building in English. We do have them, I think, available in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are three documents which have been published in 1996. The first is called "Unfinished Peace," compiled by a group of authors. Then it came out in the form of a book. It's about the visit they made in the region in 1996. They met the accused, and they found out that the situation of the two ethnic groups and the relations between Serbia, the regime of Milosevic, and the parallel system in Kosova were at a deadlock. During the meeting, they found out that the Serbs are incapable of maintaining a tolerant stand towards Albanians and negotiating with them. Another book which observed the same thing was another book speaking about the meeting with Albanian and Serb leaders and warning that the situation in Kosova was on the brink of war. Another document was that which was prepared on the basis of a meeting held between the Albanian and Serb leaders in New York, and it noted that the Albanians and the Serbs are extremely away from each other and from coming to terms regarding the definition of the status of Kosova. These were sufficient reasons to note that the situation in Kosova was serious and the political process was degenerating. And for this, Belgrade was to blame, and the accused as well, who had started -- who continued, I would say, to dramatise the problem of Kosova and transform it into his own private affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I invite you to pause there. You've identified the documents in general terms, more specifically in the statement, and they're available here for consideration by the accused or the Chamber, if necessary. You've explained their significance, that settlement seemed difficult or impossible at that time. Just then tell us this: Penultimate paragraph on the addendum statement, in the course of your work as a journalist, how complete was your survey of the relevant politicians? How many of them were you able to meet?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To be frank, Koha Ditore was the only institution free of any influence either by the Serb regime or the Democratic League of Kosova. We were an entirely independent institution, and we tried to reflect the opinions of all parties in order to make clear the prevailing views. Personally, I have conducted 21 interviews with all the Serb opposition and ruling party leaders. That is the Socialist Party, including Mihajlo Markovic, Radomir Bijodic [phoen], former Prime Minister, Vukanic -- I can't -- I don't want to number them here, but there are a total of 21 interviews, and in all of them, with the exception of two or one of them, I think, the others said that the problem of Kosova cannot be resolved without the engagement of the accused and another name very close to him, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That all the interviewees --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's, I think, all I need for the time being.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you attempt to interview the accused? Did you attempt to interview the accused's wife?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, I considered it as a very serious challenge for myself to conduct an interview with the accused, because he was the main participant in all the events in -- from 1987. But despite my insistence, I have always received a negative answer or no answer at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhiu, you will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. An exhibit number for the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you now to cross-examine this witness, bearing in mind that much of the evidence is about background matter. We've already expressed a view about that, that the relevant matter in this case concerns the indictment, and any preliminary matter is only of significance insofar as it relates to that. The political views of the witness are irrelevant, and therefore, a political argument will not be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. So if you would take this as shortly as you think proper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that the cross-examination will be limited to one hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a 92 bis witness. There was a bit added. The normal rule is one hour. We will consider at the end of it if there's any significant matter which needs covering, and also whether the hour has been spent to proper effect. So that means an absence of argument and repetition. Mr. Haxhiu -- just one moment. Just one moment. Mr. Haxhiu, could you bear in mind, please, when answering questions, that time is limited and, therefore, if you would answer as shortly as you properly can, that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted, as a preliminary, to put a question to you, because you said if the questions are appropriate. Do you mean that some of my questions were inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, because you tend to argue with the witnesses and to repeat what's been said and go over the same ground several times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to get an answer to my question. I only insist on getting an answer. I am not aware of having quarreled with any witnesses, because these false witnesses that are coming to testify do not merit me disputing -- having a dispute with them. It is now ten to ten. I'll see what I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the investigators of the Prosecution, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did, a statement that was recorded in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to an investigator whose name is Fred Abrahams; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And apart from him, there was also someone else present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please explain to the witness, if I'm asking such direct questions, that his answers have to be yes or no. I did not ask him about the presence others but only about Fred Abrahams. His answer is yes, so I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Bear that in mind, if you would, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that person introduce himself as an investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. The other person who was there present introduced himself as by this name or in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... about the other person. However, in your statement, you say that you gave that statement to the International Criminal Tribunal. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the person who interviewed you, did he introduce himself as an investigator of the Tribunal or an investigator of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He introduced himself as an investigator of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Messrs. May, Robinson, and Kwon, I wish to indicate something because Fred Abrahams, the person who appears here in the role of an investigator that the witness is referring to, that same said Fred Abrahams, is a witness testifying on behalf of Human Rights Watch here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we noted that and in due course you can ask Mr. Abrahams about it if he gives evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not asking Mr. Abrahams, I'm asking you whether someone who works at the same time as an investigator, someone who is following all trials, and witnesses are not supposed to follow trials, and who is a journalist of Human Rights Watch to appear in the role of a witness here. In how many roles can a person appear in? Only not in my case, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that when it comes to Mr. Abrahams' evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You gave your statement in English. That is what you say in the first paragraph of your statement. But in the last paragraph, on page 10, it says, certification of witness: That the witness [sic] was read out aloud to you in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I gave the statement in English. That's fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how, then, was it read out to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: These documents, which is done in English, is also translated in Albanian in this case. Every witness has a right to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am glad to hear that. Do you think that that applies to Serbian as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you made your statement in English and it was read out to you in Albanian, does that mean that the statement was not read out to you at the time you gave it but after a certain period of time, sometime later?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I gave the statement in my own home. It was recorded there. Then it was read to me in my office at Koha Ditore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After how many days?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't really remember. I don't think it was important. I really can't say how, exactly how -- when was that, after how many days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, several days later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You graduated at the faculty of law at the university in Pristina in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, it says in your statement that you graduated in 1991, that you concluded your studies in 1991. Why the difference?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did my studies at the regular university of Prishtina, but some outstanding exams which I had, I gave them in a parallel university, those exams which I couldn't take during the regular course of studies because we were driven out of the offices of the faculty of law where I was a regular student.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when were you chased out of the premises of the law faculty?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was not that we were driven out, actually, but we were not allowed to enter it in October 1981 -- in 1991. There were police forces in front of this faculty building as well as in front of other university buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you are claiming that the police would not allow Albanian students to enter the faculty premises in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question: Is it true that it was not that tuition was suspended but there was a boycott by Albanians in response to a call by separatist Albanian politicians in the country and abroad to boycott everything under state control; in education, in health, in public media, in economic enterprises and so on. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have a document here which shows that in 1990 some municipalities of Kosova, all the professors were withheld their pay, and after that, 680 professors of Prishtina municipality were likewise withheld their salaries. And this went on for 2.000 professors in Prishtina. I have documents here with me to corroborate what I'm saying as to the number of professors who have been -- who have been -- tied their hands. I have documents here. I don't see it as a boycott. It seems unreasonable for me to boycott tuition and education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We -- Mr. Haxhiu, we have the point. At the end, the Prosecution can re-examine, and if they want to bring out any points, they will. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the boycott from the period you're testifying about. You know nothing about the boycott I asked you about, nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says it wasn't a boycott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered this question. There wasn't a boycott. I'm a hundred per cent sure there was no boycott.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. And do you know why some teacher does not receive his salary? Do you know that salaries are usually not received when one doesn't perform one's duties and that salaries are linked to work? So are you claiming that those teachers and professors in schools and universities that were not receiving salaries were performing their duties and still did not receive salaries, or were they not performing their duties?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Even when they were -- when I was at school in 1990, in Decan and Podujeva and Vushtrria, the Serbian government stopped the teachers' salary. This started in 1990, let us not forget. Later this was reflected in all the towns of Kosova. I believe that the Serbian government will have evidence of this. And in 1991, only 17 per cent, only 17 per cent of schools were able to accept Albanian students, only 17 per cent of the schools of Kosova. The university buildings and high school buildings were banned to Albanians because each of them were watched by two or three policemen in front of the schools. I was a participant in these events and I am a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Don't repeat what you've already said. You claim that the policemen didn't allow you to enter. What I asked you was: Do you claim that the professors that did not receive their salaries, that they carried out their work duties and, in spite of that, did not receive their salaries? That was the point and gist of my question. Did they perform their working duties as teachers in the schools? Were they doing their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. job properly and did -- or weren't they doing their job and that's why they didn't receive salaries? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think that this is a game with words. They were unable to do their work if they were unable to enter the buildings. And when they started going to private schools, private houses, and they received their salary from the 3 per cent that was paid by the Albanians in the government of Mr. Bukoshi in exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that it wasn't that they didn't receive their salary because they didn't perform their work, but they didn't receive their salary because they were thrown out and it was made impossible for them to do their work, do their job; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I can only say one thing. The Official Gazette of Serbia laid down clearly what the school curriculum -- I can't remember the exact date, but it laid down what the plan -- the curriculum of Kosova should be. Let me give an example. In the music schools --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going some way from the point. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the school curriculum. Was the school curriculum the same for all children in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In the Prishtina musical school, you introduced about 400 songs that were in the Serbian curriculum, and this in a population that was about 90 per cent Albanian. Is this an argument to bring in 400 songs into the school of music? Let me not -- let me not even mention the issues in history lessons and other subjects of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from music, were there any other problems? You mentioned history. History, you said. So music and history, is it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, do you know how many tens of thousands of Albanian children went to the schools where tuition was in Albanian right up until 1999? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know of any Albanian, any single Albanian going to the schools organised by the Serbian government. I don't know of a single one. If you know one, give me the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they weren't going to state schools.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was impossible. It was impossible. The schools were blockaded for the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I say they weren't. Very well. That's what you claim. Okay. Now, in your statement, you speak about the fact that Rugova's representatives of the DSK party controlled the Bujku paper and that they manipulated the information distributed to Kosovo's Albanian population, propagating the illusion that Kosovo would one day achieve its independence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I said that -- you have taken this out of context in my statement, but I can say that the newspaper Bujku, in a kind of way, propagated the policies of the LDK, the Democratic League of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So before you started work to establish a new paper, this idea was propagated, that Kosovo should achieve independence?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This idea was not propagated by Bujku, but it was quite simply an idea that every Albanian in Kosova had, which was obvious. It wasn't propagated as somebody's idea, but it was the idea -- it's part of an everyday mentality of the people who have their ambitions and goals to achieve, the idea of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Independence. And in that regard, you had a clear awareness of the fact that in Kosovo there were Serbs living there too as well as Turks and Muslims and Roma and Gorani, as well as the others. What about them? Did you consider that that was of no importance?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think that in Kosova, or in a democratic political system, the majority decides in a referendum and that a part -- and it is clear that the majority ethnic group support the idea of independence and that the Serbian minority does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Kosovo is a part of Serbia. Is that something that you have in your awareness, in your consciousness? Kosovo is not a state for you to be able to speak about a majority community or a minority community. Kosovo is a part of a state, and the name of that state is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I do not know that the state of Serbia is represented in Kosova. Kosova is in the process of forming its own statehood, and Serbia, for the moment, has no presence in Kosova, whether institutional or physical. And what was once an illusion -- so now the return of Serbia to Kosova is now an illusion, just as the independence was once apparently an illusion for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now getting a long way from the indictment, Mr. Milosevic. Let's get back to the topic of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Would you answer my question, this question: Do you understand by that that you are now free?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's an irrelevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you say that Serbia cannot meddle, do you imply the occupation, a state of occupation at the moment of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That also is irrelevant. Mr. Milosevic, deal with the time with which this indictment is dealing with, not irrelevancies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from your statement, it would emerge that in a situation where independence was being propagated and in the situation in which you say you know that the Serb authorities would not allow independence - so those are the premises that you talk about - and also faced with a situation in which you know, as you yourself say that the Serb authorities will tolerate a parallel system which the Albanians have, therefore, what then, in a situation of this kind, does your option mean to accept disturbances of this kind for Kosovo to move ahead, risk shaking up the situation?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Let me only remark that the Serbian regime and the police had for years humiliated the Albanians and had assaulted their dignity. They had entered into every home. However, you, at the same time, tolerated a parallel system in Kosova which did not offer a danger of changing the situation that you had created. The second element -- element, you tolerated what we might call the -- Mr. Rugova's 32 square metres of independence. And this little enclave of independence was subjected to extreme pressure. There was the pressure of murders, of torture, and of crimes committed by your police. So you were playing a double game. And a third factor was the international community which found this situation a comfortable one, on the one hand to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm not asking about the international community now. What I'm asking you is this: I was asking you about your readiness. You say you were ready to accept violence, to opt for violence and shaking up the situation. So you were ready to opt for violence as a means of achieving your political goal. Yes or no. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't say that in my statement. I said that Kosova had to change the status quo, and the only institution that was -- which was able to move in any way was the newspaper Koha Ditore, and it was able to bring new things into this process, which didn't mean violence but activism. Because the political process in Kosova had totally degenerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that in 1991 -- you say that in 1991, the Serb police closed down the student paper Bota e Re and that you moved to the Zeri paper. How come the police closed down the Bota e Re, the student newspaper, and it didn't do this to Zeri or Bujku and the others that were well known at the time for their nationalistic and separatistic orientation and so on?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were two interventions in Bota e Re. The first one was because we published three caricatures and the police intervened, and then an article entitled "Kosova is not Serbia," and then the police intervened and imposed compulsory measures, and you, the Republic of Serbia, imposed a deputy of Assembly of Serbia as editor of Bota e Re. I will not -- for personal reasons, I will not mention this person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened? Was perhaps this publisher a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: What importance is that, when you introduce compulsory measures, whether he was an Albanian or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, this kind of argument isn't going to assist us. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm asking questions, questions that refer to what the witness talks about in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and you get into an endless argument. You have got, so far, to page 1, paragraph 3 in the English, of his statement, and you've been cross-examining for nearly half the time you're allowed. I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave Bota e Re because that same institution published the Serbian paper Zeri, so you wanted this paper to become extinguished, this student paper? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Did you leave so that Bota e Re could become extinguished because it -- there was a parallel edition of Novi Svjet in the Serbian language put out by the same institution? Therefore, you extinguished this institution and moved on to another one which was a purely Albanian institution where there was no parallel paper printed in the Serbian language. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Bota e Re was an institution where only Albanians worked. On the other hand, there was Novi Svjet where only Serbs worked. I didn't go to Zeri because there were only Albanians there, I went for other reasons which I said, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, you say in your statement that in 1991, Television Kosovo was closed down. I don't know that Television Kosovo ever existed. I know that Radio Television Pristina existed, for example, within the composition of Radio Television Serbia, but Radio Television Kosovo, that -- did it exist? Did Radio Television Kosovo exist at all?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Excuse me for this semantic nuance, but there was -- Prishtina Radio Television did exist and I said Radio Television of Kosovo. In fact, it was Prishtina Radio Television that was closed and 1.300 workers were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about Radio Television Pristina, which is within the frameworks of Radio Television Serbia just as Kosovo is within the frameworks of Serbia? Did it continue after those dates that you make mention of by broadcasting programmes in Albanian, in Serbian, in Turkish, in Romany? So what I'm asking you is did it have, throughout this time, that is to say from the time that you mentioned, did it broadcast all those programmes both in Serbian, Albanian, Turkish and Romany, in all those languages, where the editors who were Albanians, Turks, Romas, Serbs, et cetera? Did it or did it not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The programme was absolutely ridiculous. I just cannot imagine how a state like Serbia could sink so low as to employ people who were unable to read in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, if you would spare us the comment and just concentrate on the facts, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But he made a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I'm asking you if you would refrain from comment and just give us the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it yes or no? I asked you did the Radio Television Pristina have all these programmes and in all these languages, the languages of the nationalities living in Kosovo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It had programmes only in Albanian -- Serbian and Albanian and a five-minute programme in Turkish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in Serbian and in Albanian. It had programmes in those two languages and you confirm that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The Albanian programme was ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know about the network -- that's another question, whether it was ridiculous to you or not. That's a matter of criteria. We're not discussing that here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't waste time on things like that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about local stations? Did they exist? Those which broadcast in Pec, Prizren, Kosovska Mitrovica, Orahovac, Djakovica, Gnjilane, that broadcast programmes there, did those local stations exist? They didn't. All right. With editorial offices and journalists and editors who were Albanians and all these that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There was not a single radio station of that kind existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Which were the only ones, you say? Ah, I see, there were none, not a single one. Now, you say that the paper Bujku, that was under the control of Rugova's LDK, manipulated information and that it propagated the illusion that Kosovo would achieve independence and that therefore you were ready to accept the risk of shaking up the situation; shaking up the situation, disturbing the situation.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You have the translation wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually those doing the English don't make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I said we were in a position to promote the process and lead it forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I understand what you're trying to explain. Now, you say that those who gained diplomas at the parallel Albanian university had no prospects for getting jobs or moving on professionally because the state did not recognise those diplomas. That's what you say. Now, do you personally know of the case or the example of a single state that recognises the diplomas, even those from legal universities, before they are registered and recognised and certified? Do you think that a right has been violated there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any state that banishes all its pupils and -- pupils and students from its school buildings? You asked for the reasons, and I give you the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with the question. The question was the diplomas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he answered that more or less, and it's not a vital point, but he did answer it indirectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's try and move on from the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about demonstrations. And you even say that the war in Kosovo began on the 1st of October, 1998, when the students held their first peace protest and that the goal of the protest was the application of the agreement that was signed in September 1996 by Milosevic and Rugova, and then you say that the Serb side did not implement what had been agreed upon. Now, as I assume you know that it was precisely in the application of that agreement that tens of thousands of square metres were given the technical faculty, the Albanological institute and so on were handed over, and that the Serb side did in fact implement this, I'm asking you quite specifically now and concretely whether certain elements among the Albanians perhaps did not want to have the agreement applied because the agreement was signed in their name by Ibrahim Rugova whom you yourself did not recognise because, as you used to say, through his policy - and you say that on page 1 of your statement - that the DSK or LDK, whose head he was, propagated just an illusion that Kosovo would be independent and that it was necessary to move forward. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, shorten this question. It's quite impossible to deal with a question which has lasted a minute and more. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can answer because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he differs from other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There are at least two questions in that, if not more. One of them was that the Albanians did not want to implement the agreement. Now, Mr. Haxhiu, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not right. We very much wanted the agreement to be implemented, because if it were not, the process would be radicalised and the whole -- also the level of tolerance would degenerate down to zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about you personally now because you're not testifying about yourself personally. I don't think you have anything to testify about yourself personally. I'm asking you about the radical elements who endeavoured to produce violence in Kosovo. Now, were they opposed to the fact that Rugova's agreement should be successful, that the agreement signed by Ibrahim Rugova should be successful? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know what you're implying by "radical" forces. I know that we were all concerned for the agreement to be carried out, because this would show -- we see that the political process in Kosova was radicalised and the intervention against the students was fatal for the future of Kosova. It was the students who restored a fragment of the Albanians' lost dignity and disputed the occupation that you imposed in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You're now under occupation. You were not occupied then. But you were under a similar occupation during Mussolini and during Hitler. There's not much difference. Probably you felt free in those days as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a very long way from the indictment, indeed, and it's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 3 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's time for the break. Mr. Haxhiu, just to clarify one matter, you have clarified it in your second statement: Your arrest, I take it, and the various meetings took place in 1998; is that right? Not 1997.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It took place in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the date of the first protest, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 1st of October, the police entered the premises of Koha Ditore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: During the adjournment, Mr. Haxhiu, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I ought to clarify the ruling on Dr. Baccard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and make it plain that if you want to recall that witness, then it must be done by way of an addendum to his report served in the normal way and so everybody has the time to consider it and prepare, and in due course, if you want to do it, we'll consider whether we'll allow him to be recalled or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got three-quarters of an hour more, which means you'll have nearly an hour and a half with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So another three-quarters of an hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me try and be expeditious in covering these remaining questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after this agreement that we referred to a moment ago, you continued to fear a radicalisation of the situation with respect to the attitude of the Albanians towards that agreement and in respect to Kosovo in general; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After these demonstrations that you referred to, you said that it was clear that there was no possibility for a peaceful settlement in Kosovo with the Serbs and that that was the view of the Albanians. You find that on page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. I said after the unnecessary brutal intervention of the police against the students who were staging peaceful demonstrations, then I didn't see any other way out than the further radicalisation of the situation in Kosova. This was my personal view and analysis of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you personally believe, because you say that was your personal opinion, that the student demonstrations in which four persons were taken into custody and when there were certain physical contacts between the police and the students, do you believe that that was the moment when the Albanians in Kosovo were beginning the war? Was really that sufficient for the war to begin?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think that a process was needed to tackle the radicalisation of the situation. But in fact, there was a brutal intervention of the police. That was not the only case that contributed to the radicalisation of the situation. I can encounter here -- I can enumerate here many instances to prove that the radicalisation of the situation started from 1987 until the time came for the emergence of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But if on the 1st of October, 1998, you organised the demonstrations with the aim of implementing the agreement on education, tell me, then, why do you think there were demonstrations in Pristina and other places in Kosovo? For example, in 1981, which lasted for quite some time, when at the time 800 elementary and secondary schools were working, at the time more than 600 Albanian, more than ten faculty departments with separate tuition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going backwards. Just one moment. Mr. Haxhiu, just one moment. Mr. Milosevic, we're now going backwards in time, and we've had another beginning of a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to link certain things up, and my direct question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that the aim of the demonstrations on the 1st of October, 1998, was not the education agreement but, as in 1981, Kosovo Republic or an independent Kosovo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I didn't say that the participants in these demonstrations did not aspire to independence at a point in time but I said that they protested being banished from entering the premises and protesting the insult perpetrated against them for a long time. I can talk to you about the demonstrations staged on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also stated that in those days, that is in 1998, you had not even heard of the so-called KLA, and you make no mention of it in your statement. Do you know what kind of crimes and do you know of any examples of terrorism carried out by this organisation that you hadn't heard of on the 5th [sic] of October, 1998, which you indicated as being the date when the conflict in Kosovo started?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't know anything about the KLA in 1998, but I said up to the moment that the students started their demonstrations, I knew nothing about the existence of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is October 1998.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. It is October 1997, not 1998. The demonstrations started in 1997, October the 1st, but the education agreement was signed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of September, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. When was the date when you were arrested? Is it 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So up to then, up to those demonstrations, you hadn't heard of a single killing, kidnapping, or any other crime or act of terrorism by the KLA, and you hadn't heard of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I never heard of KLA up to the 26th of November, 1997. That was when I heard and I wrote for the first time my first article on the KLA, titled "Someone Has Been Fighting in Lubovec."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have devoted almost half of your statement to conversations that, together with Bakalli, as you say, had with people from the State Security Service. In those conversations, did you represent anyone in your organisation or were you participating as an ordinary citizen?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was arrested. I was interrogated in the building of the state security. After many questions, which lasted for two hours, then one of those present there asked me, "Is there someone from your side - from the Albanian side, that is - who can be our interlocutor?" I answered that, until now, all the dialogue and conversations conducted have been unsuccessful because they have been conducted by people who have been on the sidelines, and if you are really serious about holding a dialogue with us, then I can take civic courage and I will assume also my personal and public responsibility to find out -- to ensure that we establish such a dialogue, for many reasons. We had the example of Bosnia, Croatia, the murders there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just try -- Mr. Haxhiu, just try and concentrate on the questions. So the answer is that you were not representing anyone in an organisation but participating as an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a citizen. I had a responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in those conversations -- about those conversations, you regularly informed Mr. Hill, in the US embassy in Belgrade, and Mr. Norman, also a diplomat in the US embassy with whom you cooperated throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We did not cooperate. We had friendly contacts with the aim that we prevent the outbreak of a war in Kosova. That was our goal. I don't like the play of words of saying "collaboration" so it sounds rather more like a Balkan conspiracy than something which is really of interest to discuss. It is true that I had discussed this issue with Hill, Bujar Bukoshi, Fehmi Agani and others, but we discussed a crucial issue; how to stop the war from breaking out in Kosova. That was the crux of the matter. And each and every one were interested to prevent that from happening, all these people that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you're explaining this as not being cooperation but friendly relations, and I understand your explanation. But let us now clarify this point regarding your arrest. You said that you were taken to the premises of the State Security Service. However, it emerges from your statement that this was an information interview. So you were not arrested.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was right. When I was taken there, I realised that it was an information talk which, in Kosova, was a common phenomena. Tens of journalists underwent similar procedures like me. And I may say that those who were with me in that room behaved very correct with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they treated you correctly. They had this conversation with you to gain information. You were not arrested. They were courteous with you, as you yourself say in your statement, the only thing was that you were a bit nervous.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, because in light of the prevailing situation and the way I was taken from the editorial office premises, it was rather aggressive. The police came there to fetch me. But when we actually arrived there in that building, they were, as I said, very correct towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So whatever I have just said is correct. The policemen told you clearly then that they didn't want any conflict, that they wanted to take steps to avoid a conflict and so on.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my direct question now: Did they ask you to establish contact or was this something that you offered to do?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. They simply asked me if we could find the proper way to start negotiations. I promised that I will try, and then, for this, I needed to have my civic, public responsibility and courage, because in fact there was no one to stand up for Kosova. And we who knew, who were informed of what was going on, who were working in the newspaper, we received information from Serb, Albanian, international sources and we knew that it was impossible to undertake an uprising against a state machine and a military power like Serbian one was. And having this civic responsibility and courage, I said -- I promised them that I will see what I can do, because I was someone who had some influence, and I worked in an institution which was independent, like the Koha Ditore is. And Veton Surroi was another editor who also had a great influence at that time. So therefore, this was why I accepted to try and find someone who could negotiate between the Serbs and the Albanians. So I think I had enough arguments to try and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please give me a direct answer to my question, and it is a very simple one with a yes and no: Were you a cooperator of the state security or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, never. I only met your security service people three times; once in Bakalli's home, once in Brezovica, and another time when they took me and interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And they told you explicitly that they wanted to assist in establishing a dialogue to avoid a conflict; isn't that right? That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you said that the situation was extremely tense and that you were afraid of an open dialogue precisely because of the existence of extremist groups which would not approve of such a dialogue; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We tried. I gave you the reasons why I tried to do; because of what had happened in Bosnia, because the Serbian state was very powerful militarily, and there was no one to stand up for Kosova. We had tens of arguments why we should enter into dialogue, and none of -- no arguments against it. This was why we had -- we felt we had to start dialogue. And I think this dialogue did not start because people around you didn't want that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you say on page 4 that you were afraid of a frank dialogue because of extremist groups.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think that in April or May 1997, efforts were made to establish this dialogue with the Serbs. Mr. Agani tried to do with that Mr. Duhanovic and Tanic, but efforts were unsuccessful in New York and in other attempts made. Since the intervention against the students had provoked a revolt, a large scale revolt in Kosova every open form of dialogue in Belgrade or Prishtina we thought would be unsuccessful. I stated this at the peace institute in the United States, the State Department, Voice of America, in Serbian/Croatian language in an interview I gave to that radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but I was just drawing your attention to what you said, that you were afraid of a frank dialogue because of the existence of extremist groups. That is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his explanation. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you attended the conversations conducted by Stanisic with Bakalli and you.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, we held another meeting with Gajic and Hadic, whom we never invited nor asked to come, but they offered to come, thinking -- we thought that Mr. Stanisic is part of the group. But when we saw them coming to Bakalli's home, we couldn't turn them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, just deal with the questions you're asked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Stanisic make any threats against you at those meetings or was he -- did he treat you decently and enter into a dialogue with you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Hadic were very severe with us. I think they came to Bakalli's home to show their force. They referred to projects which were shocking to us. Stanisic was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Stanisic did not threaten you.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Only Hadic kept pointing his finger at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the meeting with Stanisic. Very well. So Stanisic did not threaten you with any kind of violence against the Albanians. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Let me go back and make a digression. Stanisic said that we won't accept the option you offered, which was Kosova Republic. He said there is no one around Milosevic who will accept this alternative, and I am saying you that if you pursue it, we will end up in war. That was expressly what Stanisic said. But he also said that, "I will personally see to it that you have your university and academy. But as to the status of Kosova Republic, forget about that. There are nationalist people around Milosevic who will invoke a war if you ask for that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Please. I asked you a very clear question. Stanisic did not threaten you with any kind of violence against the Albanians during those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I am asking this because he is the only participant apart from Mr. Bakalli, Mr. May. And Bakalli explained here that Stanisic allegedly threatened them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You put the matter -- you put the matter to him and he has -- Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he's answered in the words which Stanisic used. Now, that is an answer to the question. Now, Mr. Haxhiu, what do you want to add, briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just I want to answer this: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakalli said here that not Stanisic but Gajic and Hadic said -- and threatened 600 and -- 463 villages which would be burnt, "If you did not give up the options you put forward." Stanisic did not mention the burnt villages, but it was the two representatives who came at the meeting with Stanisic. I can say that they were both fat bureaucrats, and their position was a stupid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But Stanisic was the main speaker, not they, and he did not make any threats to you, and we can confirm that and move on. To go back to Koha Ditore, you say that in March 1999, it was punished. On the 22nd of March, it was fined 500.000 dinars. You called this a disgrace for the international minister, who started proceedings in the court in which you were fined; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was sentenced to four -- 435.000 marks equivalent in dinars, and I consider this to be a disgrace for a minister of information. More over, the judge who sentenced me told me that he was obliged to give me the sentence because this had come from Belgrade. And this was the main issue for me, because he had no evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says that you were fined 500.000 dinars. That is what you told the Beta agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you fined 500.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I want to find it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. May, in the second statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isn't this a statement on his part when he says it is correct that he was fined 500.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will get on better, if you are cross-examining on a statement, if you tell the Court where it is that you're referring to. It's fair to the witness, but it's also important that we can follow the points that you're trying to make. Now, I've yet to find where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help? The addendum has a reference to the fine on the second page, the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness has confirmed that he was fined 500.000 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I was able to understand from information I received, 410 was the fine for your newspaper and 110 you personally.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know what the dinar equivalent is, but that seems to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 500.000 dinars, the equivalent in German marks. If you remember in 1999 the rate of exchange was 13 dinars to one German mark, so it could have been a couple of tens of thousands of marks. Isn't that so? So not 200.000 marks, as it says here, if I said it -- if I saw it correctly. Whether it is in the addendum or somewhere else, I don't know, I'm not sure. Yes, in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have the point. We have -- we have the point. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we've cleared that up as well.
