The newspaper was fined because of articles it carried, and the media wrote that the proceedings were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. instituted because the article provoked a national intolerance. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Information we got from the court, that is true, but we don't know with what article we incited racial hatred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were punished for provoking national intolerance and hatred, and in your statement to the Beta agency, you called it a disgrace for the minister of information of Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So less than a year after that, on the 9th of February, 2000, the head of the civilian mission in the UN, Mr. Kouchner, issued a decree, saying that anyone who publicly provokes hatred, conflict, or intolerance between ethnic groups will be fined heavily, up to a prison term of five years, and in special circumstances, it can go up to eight years, and if it is systematically done, up to ten years of prison. So I assume you're familiar with that decree. How then do you feel as an intellectual, a journalist, a free journalist, a fighter for the freedom of the press, consider this fine of a couple of thousand German marks, you call this a disgrace, and here you have this same matter sanctioned by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is turning into a speech. Now, what is the question? Put it shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question could roughly be the following: How did it happen that in less than a year you should be transformed to such an extent that the fine of 400.000 dinars for you -- for your newspaper and 110.000 dinars for you personally, you call it a disgrace, and a decree that provides for punishment up to ten years you consider acceptable?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The question of Kouchner has never been the means to punish any journalist because there has never been any need, just as no Serbian government ever sentenced Hashim Thaci for his news conferences. And we reported Hashim Thaci's news conferences in our newspaper. So why should I be convicted for carrying them in the paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now moving into the realms of irrelevance. If you want to ask him about that particular incident, you can, but trying to compare it with other matters does not assist. I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move on so as not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were informed about the beginning of the bombing and that you then went to Tetovo, Macedonia, and continued to publish your newspaper there?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell the truth, after the 18th of March, I wore a shirt reading "NATO, just do it." And even today, it seems to me incomprehensible why we didn't sign Rambouillet and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Haxhiu, about going to Tetovo and continuing to publish. Now, will you please deal with that question and that alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I left Kosova on the 2nd of April, and I was in a cellar in Kodra e Diellit neighbourhood, and there were -- with 30.000 inhabitants of that neighbourhood. We were all expelled on the same day, with a family and a child whom I did not know, and we travelled to Tetovo by car and came out in Macedonia. In Macedonia, I organised the newspaper Koha Ditore in exile, and this was distributed to the refugees in the camps in Macedonia and in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We finally got an answer to my question. You fled to Macedonia and you continued to publish the newspaper in Macedonia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I didn't flee. I was expelled. The whole neighbourhood was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not argue about that. He said he was expelled. It's quite plain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only five days after the beginning of the NATO aggression on the 29th of March, there was a report that you had been killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it on television when I was in the cellar. And I think it was Komodor Velbi [phoen] who made a statement saying that, in Kosova, Fehmi Agani, Baton Haxhiu and three other intellectuals had been executed. I heard the report as other people did. I don't know where the information came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My question is: At the time, you were in Macedonia, and on the 7th of April --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. On the 29th, NATO stated that I was dead, at a news conference. I at that time was in a cellar in Kodra e Diellit in Prishtina, with three families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of April, you stated for the independence that you could not deny the report on the radio because you had to hide for five days in a basement in Pristina. That's what you stated. And if on the 7th of April you were already in London and you made yourself heard in London, does that mean that you went to London straight from that cellar or did you first go to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: After the cellar, we were four days in the hills near the border with Tetovo, and we left Kosova, and on the next day I went to Germany and met German Foreign Minister Mr. Fischer, and immediately from Germany I flew to London and met Mr. Cook with a group of intellectuals, and then until the 18th of April I went to France and met the French Foreign Minister. And I didn't stay a single day in Macedonia after arriving there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you deny this false NATO report that you had been executed by the Serbs? When did you deny that report?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I denied this on the 6th or the 7th of April on Deutsche Welle, at the 1530 broadcast, because the telephone links with Prishtina were cut and it was impossible to phone. And third, I was very frightened of announcing that I was alive. This is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What you want to say -- what you're saying is that you were late in denying it, not because you were saving credibility of NATO information, these false ones, but because physically you weren't able to make a statement earlier, before the 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It seems a rather sad statement to make, but everybody in Kosova at that time was dead. We were impotent, in cellars, and with no idea of what would happen to us. Anybody who was announced as being dead, this was a useful and relevant kind of information at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: In what capacity were you in the state of Virginia in July 2000; as a member of the delegation of Albanians or as a journalist? In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were two meetings, in Eli House in Washington and at Lansdowne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was just asking you in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I represented civil society. I have the documents with me, and you can see what I presented in -- at Eli House and at Lansdowne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On the 26th of May, 1999, you took part, in the throes of the bombing in Yugoslavia, in Ljubljana at a meeting called Who is that Singing There? It was the fund opened by the association of Slovenia while your paper was coming out in Macedonia, and at that time you praised the NATO bombing; is that right? You supported it. Now, do you consider, Mr. Haxhiu, with all these activities of yours, that you were a part of the scenario not to support any kind of negotiations or, rather, to give a pretext for the NATO pact aggression against Yugoslavia? Do you consider that you were part of that scenario and a participant in that scenario?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Can I ask something? Why did not you, the Serbian delegation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just try and deal with his questions. What is suggested, it appears, is that you were a part of -- part of a scenario, it's described, that was set up, which seems to be some sort of conspiracy which was set up to give a pretext for the NATO aggression, as it's called, against Yugoslavia. Now, was there any conspiracy, plan, or pretext of that sort?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. This is the Balkan mentality. People in the Balkans always think of conspiracies. Life in the Balkans is a conspiracy. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Not to waste time. You said no, so let's move on. Now, at the time you're describing on page 5 of your statement, you say: "It was clear to all the Albanians that to demand full independence could lead to war and that moderate Albanians had the position that to demand independence can lead to war."

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We considered that the problem of the status of Kosova would be solved by a process, and the insistence on immediate independence led to conflicts, and we asked for a process in a very sophisticated and continual fashion, and indeed a dignified manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You indicate the existence of great demands for independence and that an obstacle to the public negotiations was fear of extremist groups therefor, that is to say groups in favour of the use of violence in order to achieve their political goals; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I would like to explain. Please do not take matters out of context. We are not dealing with extremist forces here or the threat of extremist forces. We are dealing with your lack of will and your -- the lack of will on your staff to solve the problem of Kosova. That's clear. You personally dramatised and made an icon out of Kosova as a problem, and the obstacle was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what I'm claiming is not correct; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as you mentioned the Koha Ditore paper, is it correct that Ibrahim Rugova called upon the citizens of Suva Reka to join the KLA and give contribution to the fund to finance the KLA and that this was in the summer of 1998 in that paper, through that paper?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Rugova did not like to mention the KLA, and Rugova mentioned the KLA after the war, and this statement does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the talk you said you had with the representatives of the security service, as far as I was able to understand on page 7, last paragraph, they mentioned armed Albanians fighting against the state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The KLA was not mentioned. Armed groups were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fighting against the state. Well, the KLA is the so-called KLA because it was a terrorist organisation, in fact. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That's your idea. I think that the KLA was the product of the incessant repression by the Serbian state, and a group that, in a way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go into that. We're not going to go into that for the moment, the various characterisations. You were asking about the meeting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say at the end of 1977 [sic], no Albanian wanted to accept any kind of autonomy or any kind of negotiation except about independence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1997.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The ultimatum for an independence was something that every Albanian wished for, and you knew that any solution to the status quo of Kosovo would lead to an open conflict, and you talk about that in the appendix to -- addendum to your statement, and it is the Prosecution number 030363047; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Could you put the question again? Because it's not very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it has to do with the fact that you said that no Albanian wanted to accept anything but independence; is that right? And then --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were -- there was an element of flexibility in this, but there was not a lot of courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Through violence, then. And that conflict is something that you wished for and wished to provoke. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With some structures in the West. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. This is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It isn't. All right. Now, it was your position that regardless of who was at the head of Serbia, that the problem was in fact Serbia and that it was the Serbian mentality when it came to the relationship towards Kosovo. So your position was that I was created by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. There was an article I published in a book called "Kosova" in Washington --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, we're getting away from the indictment. Mr. Milosevic, your time is coming to an end. You can ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have five more minutes, as far as I can see here, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you haven't. You have one more question and then you will have had your 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I must now refer to the addendum to the statement in English that I received last night, with just a few points, just a few points, please. I'm not going to take up much time in discussing it. So you said that you saw me in Slovenia in 1990 and you were among a group of journalists when there was the conference of six representatives of the republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We were just this kind of distance from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As a journalist asking questions, then. And you say here that you asked me a question, and it was: "When would Kosovo Albanians be handed self-determination in Kosovo Republic?" That's what it says here in the statement.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago when you were talking, you said that you had asked me, "When are you going to leave behind the chauvinist positions and give us Albanians the right to self-determination," et cetera, et cetera, which is something that you don't make mention of in your statement and I'm sure you couldn't have asked me something like that at the time using those words and that language but let's go back --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Of course look at the transcript, because you are -- a hundred per cent you were asked this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, please, do you consider that national minorities, that ethnic minorities in any country can, by expressing their rights to self-determination, secede from that state?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This is a dogmatic view. I don't think we should dwell on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The views of the witness are not relevant. Now, you've got one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many European states would fall apart if their national minorities had the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If those are the questions you're going to ask, I'm bringing this to an end. Mr. Kay, have you any questions? No. Mr. Milosevic, you've had more than enough chance. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three more minutes, and it refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to ask Mr. Kay if he has any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the second statement of the witness, served 22nd May, and I'm looking at the passage which reads as follows. I'll read it out for your benefit, Mr. Haxhiu. "It is my opinion that the birth of the KLA was the product of Serbian repression towards Albanians, of inert international policy, and of Ibrahim Rugova's desire to preserve the status quo. After the Prekaz massacre in 1998, the KLA grew from a very small number to more than 20.000 men under arms." And it's that matter that I want to ask you questions about. Do you understand? It seems that there was a rapid growth of the strength of the KLA from 1998 to 1999. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say that there were 20.000 men under arms, in what context do you mean that? Twenty thousand as a military force or 20.000 dispersed between military and living as civilians? Can you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I may explain it. In 1997, when I wrote an article in my newspaper, I didn't see more than 100, let's say, KLA soldiers. Following the Prekaz and Likoshan massacres, the revolt spread out all over Kosova and everyone thought it could find solutions by taking to the mountains and they rallied around this armed group which was called KLA. We think that this was the first step to restitute a lost dignity and fie the occupation, Serb occupation of Kosova. And the growth in number of the KLA is due to the murders perpetrated against children, women, elderly. This is the response of every Albanian who thought that some resistance should be put up to the Serb regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've given us a lot of background there. I'm interested in detail. So please don't repeat the background again as we waste time.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We understand what you would say, all right? So 20.000 men, then, is that men in the hills, with weapons? Is that what you mean? Not citizens living in villages? How do you put that figure of 20.000?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: A group of journalists, international journalists, and some of us visited the mountains near Malisheva. There was a burial ceremony there. We saw a long line of people -- of soldiers and males who were waiting to be -- to join the KLA. I can't say accurately whether -- if there was -- if there were 20.000 people, but something like that. It was in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Twenty thousand men under arms, and presumably the support for the KLA, including those not under arms, you would put as a bigger figure again?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I didn't say that all of them were armed, but some of them were sympathisers. Some were members of the KLA. Some were dressed in civilian clothes, some of them were dressed in military uniforms and with the KLA logo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered my last question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters arising in relation to the questions asked by Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The restoration of dignity by the KLA - it's also in the second statement you made - what had removed the dignity of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The dignity of the Albanians was broken. They were debased in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kosova. They started in 1987. Just to give you some examples, constitutional amendments --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The constitutional amendments by force, the isolation of 300 intellectuals, banishing students from entering school premises, systematic repression, and the entry of police forces in every house, failing to implement the education agreement, the generation of the political process in Kosova, the fleeing of 500.000 Albanians from Kosova up to 1997 because they didn't find employment there, and the brutal intervention against the students; all this led up to the establishment of the KLA which in some way restored our dignity and contested the occupation, Serb occupation of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to a few questions arising from questions of the accused. It was suggested at one stage that you had been ready to opt for violence. Just yes or no, had you personally been ever ready to opt for violence?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, never. Never were we in favour of violence. We always were in favour of peaceful solutions. I have done this also in my site that I have opened on the Internet to promote Serb/Albanian dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were anxious at one stage in the questioning to say something about the Albanian language television programme. I'd like you to confine your answer to one sentence and preferably a short one: What was the characteristic of the Albanian language television output that you found unsatisfactory?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think when it -- the television was closed and replaced by the Albanian speakers. I don't know where they found those people, but the syntax of the Albanian language they used was outdated, incomprehensible, and the translations were absolutely translations using a Serb syntax.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it an output that was likely to impress and cheer Albanian listeners or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This was done in the framework of a Goebbels plan initiated by Serb nationalists and translated in Albanian by Albanian speakers who were working in the Radio Television of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Tanic, you spoke of his being involved in negotiations. To what degree was he a serious participant in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Tanic was -- we were together with Mr. Tanic and a group of Serbs in 1992 in Orid [phoen] at a conference organised by Boris Vukobrad, in Paris. I never met that person ever since, but the way he talked about the problems seemed -- gave me the impression that he was well-informed about the situation and the Kosova issue because he had a friend in Belgrade who was an Albanian journalist, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... was he actually -- was he participating in the discussions in a serious way?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it correct in answer to a question from His Honour Judge Kwon, a detail about --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, [Interpretation] he was -- Mr. Mihajlovic and Tanic kept constant contact with Fehmi Agani as of 1993, and as the man who kept the contacts between them was Farim Strihiu [phoen], an Albanian journalist in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You corrected a date about your arrest, or you clarified a date about your arrest. Just for the avoidance of any doubt, in your statement, you speak of your understanding being that the war began on the 1st of October of a particular year. What year do you say it was that the war really began?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Politically speaking, the war started after the intervention of the Serb police against the students in the fictitious sense of the word but in real terms, it started with the massacre perpetrated against Likoshan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the meeting with Stanisic and the two more heavily-built men who made threats that you described as not serious, did Stanisic expressly dissociate himself from the threats of the other two men, including the man Hadic?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Stanisic was aware of all what was said by Gajic and Hadic. Mr. Hadic was very arrogant, very brutal, and he turned towards me and said, "If you make this public, then you will end up where you deserve." Mr. Hadic -- in fact this group that is composed of two bureaucrats, was very brutal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did Stanisic dissociate himself from the threats to which they referred?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then two last questions, one about the fine. There was a certain amount of room for uncertainty, I think. You've set out in your addendum statement, in Deutschmarks, a figure for how much you say the newspaper was fined and how much you were fined. The accused has drawn your attention to the figure of 200.000 Deutschmarks. Can you remember or tell us how much the fines were?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you cannot understand the inflation rates -- rate then in Yugoslavian state. Deutschmark kept fluctuating. Within a day, this inflation, for example, was 40.000 -- worth 40.000 Deutschmarks that day. On the next day or after two or three days, it went down to 25.000 Deutschmarks. So under these conditions, it's very difficult for me to give a precise figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But as to whether it was a very substantial sum of money, as 200.000 Deutschmarks would always be, or a much more modest sum of the scale the accused is suggesting is reflected, what do you say? Was it a substantial fine or a comparatively trivial one?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was very high fine. Earlier on, two other newspapers in Belgrade were fined. I think it was Vreme and Danas, if I'm right. I'm not sure about Danas. The third newspaper to be fined and warned to be closed down was Koha Ditore, but we were unable to pay that amount of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the fine has never been paid, has it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The judge told you that he had to fine you because he was told to do so by Belgrade. That's the way you put it in evidence. Did the -- without guessing, first of all, did the judge explain things in any more detail than that or were these exactly the words he used?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I said Bajram Kelmendi was my lawyer two days before he was murdered, and he addressed Mr. Kelmendi. He said, "Mr. Kelmendi, I know that this is not right, not just, but I have received orders from Belgrade and I have to carry out the order." Even though it was Sunday, a holiday, they took us to the judge's office to communicate the decision that we were fined because of an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you - just yes or no to this, please - did you understand what he meant by saying that Belgrade had given this instruction? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, we understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. It was just yes or no. Would that understanding be based on previous experience of a similar kind or would it be based on a general understanding of the political situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I think that there were similar occasions going on -- cases going on in Kosova courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have - and again just yes or no - do you have any hard evidence to show where the instructions from Belgrade were coming from, whether they were coming from the judiciary, from the administration, from an individual, from another body? Just yes or no, do you have hard evidence to say where the instructions were coming from?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. I can't say, but this is what he told us. "I have orders from Belgrade." He didn't show us any proof or any evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm obviously content to go and ask the next question but in the circumstances unless the Chamber wants me to, I don't think I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, you were asked about connections to NATO at the time that you'd been reported as dead when you were in fact in hiding. At the time that you were in hiding, did you have any connection, practical, whether by radio or otherwise, with NATO or any members of NATO?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I have never had any connections with NATO, neither did I have any physical possibilities to communicate with my neighbour, let alone with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I ask arising from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, up to quite recently, you were known to us under a pseudonym as K28. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Didn't you apply for the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were there any threats or danger in regards to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. There has never been any threats because I've never had anything to hide. Some media has written some prattle about me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Nice could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll make clarify that. I'll make inquiries and clarify, perhaps after the break, and I'll certainly I'll retain the witness long enough to ensure that anything that arises from the clarification can be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, that apart, in case there are any questions about that, but apart from that, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is one to whom I had hoped to speak this morning before he came to give evidence. In the event, I haven't done so and haven't been able to ask him a couple of questions arising from his summary that I would prefer to do. I don't think it's possible. And the summary has just been served. It's a rather long summary but I'm happy to tell the Chamber that nearly all of the material in the early pages has been covered by other witnesses and so I'll be able to go through it very quickly. It's one of those statements that might conceivably have been dealt with on a partial 92 bis basis but we decided, in light of his position, not to. So I was going to wonder if the Chamber might consider taking a slightly earlier than usual break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I make a correction to something I said this morning in relation to Dr. Baccard's possible giving of evidence about the other report, other forensic report. I said that that evidence had been disclosed. The position is that it was disclosed in full and in colour to the amici on the 6th of February. At that time, a black and white copy only was served on the accused because he wasn't looking at or using his materials at all and it was thought better to save the colour version for provision to him at a time when it became more likely to be useful to him. His approach has, of course, now changed, as we now know. We will -- we are in a position and will serve the colour version on him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But as far as I understand it, Dr. Baccard's comments are something knew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. They'll have to be the subject of a further report if we decide that we wish to seek to add his evidence at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that seems to me the proper way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we do that, if we do that today, we'll be in time within 30 days from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please. Can we have your full -- it may be a good idea if the witness puts the headphones on, I think. I know you understand English.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It's okay. It's okay for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: My name is Adnan Merovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the summary that's been provided in 12 pages, I think it is, is one that I can deal with, I think, very summarily so far as the first six or seven pages is concerned. As to background, I hope I may be permitted to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you born in the Vucitrn area, studying electrotechnical engineering at Pristina, graduating in 1981, thereafter working for the Associated Bank of Kosovo in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1983, did you start compulsory military service which you completed, returning to your job in the bank until 1990, when you were dismissed in circumstances we'll hear about shortly? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as we're going to discover, you were, for several years, the personal assistant to Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, the witness who we saw a few weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By way of clarification and in order to explain why I'm skipping over certain paragraphs, Your Honour, although the witness deals with the Kosovo Polje events in paragraph 2, Mr. Merovci, were you actually present there yourself or not?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, I was not present personally, but I followed it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I can go to paragraph 3, the background of ethnic tensions. Before you lost your job, while you were still at work, in work was there any deference of one side to the other? If so, how? Or of one group to the other.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At the time we're talking about, that's after 1981, relations at work and human relations between the Serbs and Albanians were tense. And the Albanians respected the Serbs in daily life and at work. Personally, I worked in an office with members of the Serbian community, and we were very polite to them. I can cite only one example in a group whenever a meeting was held and there was only one Serb was present, the Serbian language was used so that one person in the middle of ten others should not feel discriminated against.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 but over the page. Television output, did it have any effect on relations between Albanian Serbs -- Albanians and Serbs? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this time, propaganda in the mass media had its effect. It was propaganda dictated from above, and it was propaganda that treated the Albanians as second-class citizens, and it favoured the Serbs and described the Albanians as a people perpetrating injustices against the Serbs. This is what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us, just in a sentence, what if any would be the effect of such output on relationships at work in a mixed community on the day or days following output of the type you've described.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In fact, at this time, relations were at a minimum and might be described as proper on the surface, but they were in fact tense because of the events of these times and because of the propaganda that was directed from above. And any event that happened was described in a false way and this had an effect on working relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a great deal about the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy, and we've heard of the arrest of the man Vllasi. After his arrest, was there a movement of Serbs into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As I said, the initiative, the constitutional changes were issued for public discussion, and the people of Kosova expressed their discontent at the prospect of these changes. And at this time I was employed in the bank and was a member of the Independent Trade Union which mainly dealt with workers' rights. And we, too, as bank workers, expressed our discontent at the constitutional changes, the changes to the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement and in the summary the speech at Gazimestan, but again were you present? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If -- if I may be allowed, the previous question you mentioned Vllasi, who was the political boss of Kosova and the man who in the political structures mounted the greatest opposition to the constitutional changes, and he paid with prison for all the things he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But we've had this evidence, you see, from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] As for Gazimestan, this was an event of a nationalist character. It was an event involving --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... follow what may seem to you to be tedious instructions. Yes or no, were you there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had the evidence from other witnesses, so unless you're asked about it by the accused, I'll move on. We know of the creation of the LDK party. Did you become active in it from an early stage, and indeed, did you take the position initially as part-time assistant to Dr. Rugova while you were still working at the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: From the foundation of the Democratic League of Kosova on the 21st of October, 1989, I was an activist or a part-time activist. And when I was dismissed from my job, I became a very involved activist, involved full-time in the work of the LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move towards the loss of your job, but first of all, tell us this: At work, were you a member of the trade union, and indeed did you hold office in the trade union at the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. We tried -- we tried hard to defend workers' rights because this was a period when the rights of Albanian workers, too, were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, 1989, were there measures that I think you described as emergency measures in place, and if so, what effect did they have on Albanian employees at work?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was a time when the Serbian regime wanted to take economic control of Kosova, and in this sense, in the bank where I worked, emergency measures were imposed, and as a result of this step, about 300 workers were dismissed in the entire organisation of the bank, and only 60 Albanians were left, and not one Serb was dismissed from his job at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of other things: The measures of which you speak, did Albanians have to indicate their acceptance of those measures in some particular way?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In fact, these measures were of an entirely political character, and the imposed management was directed by the regime and tried by means of some simple operations, supposedly merely of a contractual nature, to dismiss the Albanians en masse. I could produce evidence of this. In one case, the imposed authorities tried -- tried to dismiss all the workers from the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the question: How did the Albanian workers have to show they acknowledged, if this is the case, these emergency measures?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The Albanians understood these measures as being political ones, even though, in the bank where I worked, they tried to explain them as a part of -- part of the bank accountancy measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's my mistake for not being clear, obviously. I'm going to move on. It may not apply to people in the bank but was there anything a person had to wear to show their acknowledgement of measures?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Sixty workers were left from 400 previously, and they were all mainly experts in their professions without whom the bank wouldn't have been able to work. And I was one of them to start with, for a few days --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: -- because I used to work in the computer centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not making myself clear. My fault, Mr. Merovci. We're just going to move on, I think. Despite the cut in number of Albanian employees, were other workers taken on in the bank, and if so, what nationality or what group were they from?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this time, there were cases in which other employees were taken on, and these were Serbs. And not a single Albanian, as I said before, was ever employed later, and not a single Serb was dismissed. On the contrary, we have cases in which other Serbs were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did these new Serbs find to live when they got a job in the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. These incoming Serb workers at the bank, where did they find to live?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: These people who were employed, we're now talking only about the time when emergency measures were taken, because some Serbs indeed even came before this time as part of the programme to bring Serbs to Kosova, and there were Serbs brought from Serbia; and in my office, sometime around about 1986, a colleague of mine came who knew nothing about the job but who had every privilege, and he was not competent and decided to leave himself. His name was Budimir Kavacic, and he was a chemist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, again probably my fault, but the simple question was where did they find to live; how did they find apartments, matters of that sort? And you've replied how they had every privilege.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: They came and lived in flats assigned to them by the company, mainly outside Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you lost your job, as you've already told us. What was the cause, what caused you to lose your job?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was involved in the computer centre, and I was removed along with all the other Albanians in the bank because of the bank clearance system, but a few days before, my supervisor summoned me to his office and said that, "You will have to choose between your job and politics," because he had seen me on television with Mr. Rugova. And my response was, "This has no effect on the work I do, and my political activities are free and are my personal affair." But after this, the following day I received the decision on my desk for my dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Albanian police officers, were any of those to lose their jobs? Were any retained? And if so, on what terms?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The police of Kosova, which had been largely Albanian, most of them left their work, refusing the orders brought by Belgrade. There were some who were dismissed in various different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 13. Dr. Rugova was to become president following a referendum. And did you become his full-time assistant or personal secretary?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In 1992, that is after the referendum, there were presidential and parliamentary elections, and I was a person who was a close colleague, in the technical sense, of Mr. Rugova. I was his personal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the result of those elections, how do you say they were dealt with by the authorities in Belgrade? Were they -- were they recognised? Were they tolerated? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The Democratic League of Kosova was formed as a result of the tolerance extended to the pluralist system in the old federation. It was what you might call a bona fide party. And after this, elections were held, but these elections were not accepted by the regime and nor were they internationally recognised. But nevertheless, these elections were a continuation of the institutions of Kosova under the previous system so that there would not be an institutional vacuum. And the absolute majority of Kosova citizens organised elections at which the LDK and Rugova won a majority and Mr. Rugova won an absolute majority as president of the Republic of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 14. In the late spring or early summer of 1995, did you find yourself in the police headquarters of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's true. In 1995, I was summoned by the Serbian secret service in Prishtina to what was called an interview for three days, three successive days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The apparent objective of those interviewing you being what?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The pretext to summon me was an absurd one and was not what the real purpose of the interview was. The real purpose was to ascribe to my work and through me to the -- to Dr. Rugova and to implicate Dr. Rugova in a supposed creation of a Ministry of Interior which was not part of the Republic of Kosova at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were interviewed for three days but you were not detained further?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was held for three days, and after three days, I was released without being imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you presented with any document to sign in the course of this exercise?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this time, my position near to Mr. Rugova was very important to the security service, and most Albanians summoned to interviews of this kind were offered the chance of cooperating with the security service. And it was sort of offered to me but in a more subtle way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on from that. In September 1995, did you find yourself involved with the police when you did land up spending time in custody?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. In September of the same year, that is 1995, I was summoned by the same service. I refused to go there without having an official warrant. Then they warned me that they would resort to other means and ways. And one day the police stopped me on the street and told me to go there, and from there I -- there I was arrested. After the arrest -- this was a Thursday. It was not a coincidence, but it was deliberately done to detain us there during the weekend. And on Monday, they continued -- they said I would be staying -- and they kept me there for 30 days on the pretext that I was in possession - I don't remember even today - on possession of arms, of an arm, that is, three, four years ago. In fact, I offered to buy an arm, which was never found on me, was never confiscated, and was never used by me but in a statement of a person whom I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't want to retry the whole issue. Were you eventually imprisoned for six months?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I was imprisoned. My lawyer, the late Bajram Kelmendi, appealed for my release, and I was released after 60 days. And my family to pay to put in my houses as a guarantee for my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was the conviction dealt with on appeal and was it overturned?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: After this time, the second instance court refused -- revoked this punishment. Then I was sentenced to six months of probation, but it was revoked by the second instance court on account of absence of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to move on from that. Thank you. Paragraph 16 I can deal with briefly. We've heard about the education agreement, we've heard about the meeting of Dr. Rugova and the accused at the White Palace. I think you went there but you stayed outside with the accused's chief of security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 17. By 1998, were you concerned that you and Dr. Rugova were being followed from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you calculate what was the reason for your being followed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I think that we were being followed by secret services which knew everything about our activity in details. I have noted that. The Democratic League of Kosova was a legal party, and it made use of this possibility for conducting legal activities, which in my view were a jewel, I would say. So in this way, there were very few pretexts or reasons for mistreating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why do you think they were following you or why were you being followed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Because I was a key person in the technical structure of the president, the then-president of the Republic of Kosova's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you can speak, if asked, about the treatment you received at the Macedonian border on your return to Kosovo from trips abroad.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't worry about that now. Just yes, and if anybody wants to know, they can ask you.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise at paragraph 19, did you become aware of what seemed to you a build-up of troops of the VJ near Suva Reka at one stage?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, you can answer detailed questions about that, if asked. Was there an agreement between the accused following meetings or following meetings of Dr. Rugova with the American Ambassador Walker? Was there an agreement to withdraw troops?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The agreement between the accused and the -- Mr. Rugova, there wasn't at that time. It was an agreement between the accused and Mr. Holbrooke, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you -- were you aware of the terms of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was aware as much as I could through the media. I knew that it was an agreement on reducing as much as possible the Serb forces in Kosova, and on allowing a Verification Mission of the OSCE led by Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get regular reports from the Kosovo information centre that enabled you to check whether the accused was sticking to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The centre for information in Kosova was an institution to provide information to the public in all areas, mainly about the developments at that time, and we had correspondence covering all the parts of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the terms of the agreement the accused had made with Ambassador Holbrooke being honoured?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In fact, this agreement was never made public to -- in details, but only it was referred to. Opinions were given about it. And we saw that a commission of the OSCE verification in Kosova was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You went to Rambouillet as head of the Federal Secretariat, I think?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I was part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a lot about that so we're going to go over to page 6 and paragraph 23. Was everybody bar one person of the Albanian delegation ready to sign the agreement at the conclusion of the talks?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In the first attempts made by the Kosova delegation, which worked jointly with the others, there was in fact minimal consensus reached, with the exception of Mr. Thaci, who had his reservations and who for some days kept postponing the signing of this agreement. In fact, it was not signed at that meeting. It was -- a letter of intent was signed, saying that the actual agreement would be signed in two weeks' time, after consultations to be held in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time and between then and the later meetings in Paris, I think, did you notice a change in the level of troops in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this two weeks' period, which in fact turned out to be three weeks, despite the Holbrooke agreement, the Serb forces made use of this period to occupy Kosova. Normally, these forces came mainly in the night. And I can prove their deployment with the reports of our correspondents who kept reporting on their movements all over Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same period of time, did you notice a change in the composition of the police units or in their presence in the area?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The Serb forces and what we could see in the streets intensified the so-called notorious checkpoints, as they call them. The structure of the police force was various, that is in terms of uniforms and technique and armaments they used or carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Typically, how were they dressed, the police who you noticed at this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: They were police donned in uniforms, in combat alertness. They wore green uniforms, blue uniforms, while the special forces usually wore green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So then we come to the Paris meeting. We've heard about that so I needn't trouble you with it save for this: Following the meeting, did you travel to Brussels and meet General Wesley Clark? Paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't travel there, but the other group went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I needn't trouble you with that. On your return from Paris, I think you went first to Tirana in Albania.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went and found your way back into Kosovo. Did you notice Albanians already leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During my trip from Skopje to Prishtina, through the border of Hani i Elezit, we were the only ones travelling, going into Kosova by car. And we saw many cars leaving Kosova. They were mainly cars belonging to foreign organisations and civilians who were leaving Kosova with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you notice VJ personnel at tunnels on the highway?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. But they were invisible, so to say, because it was a latent period, we then trying to pretend that everything was in order in Kosova, but in essence, the situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you actually see the VJ personnel doing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: They were hiding, mainly in the mountains. I saw them on the road from Hani i Elezit to Prishtina, and in one instance, they stopped us at the crossroads leading to Viti. They conducted a routine check on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see them doing anything at any tunnel, please?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When we entered Prishtina, we saw that Prishtina was unlike before, with a fear prevailing everywhere. And we saw the presence of Serb forces like never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you can't remember anything special about what they were doing at any tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Are you talking about the day when we returned? This is all I saw. If you are asking me about the period up to the beginning of the NATO airstrikes, because we returned on the 21st and the bombing started on the 24th. During these three days, the situation was very tense and insecurity reigned everywhere. This was due to the demonstration of military and police force and their movements and activities, as I said, which were never seen before. And to be more specific, they were present mainly in public places where people usually go, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to get this particular point. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 29. When you got back to Pristina, did you see any irregular or paramilitary forces, and if so, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. We saw people carrying different weapons, civilians, people without hats with green jackets, as if they belonged to some formations, with their weapons on their shoulders, or sometimes they carried it on their hand and demonstrating, making their presence very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, more particularly, if anything, were they doing to property or to people?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During those days, in public places, in bakeries where people lined up to get loaves of bread or in various restaurants, coffeeshops, they started to show off their force and to destroy these places that belonged to the Albanians in Prishtina. This was the time when many explosions occurred and many restaurants and coffeeshops were destroyed which belonged to the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had there been a cellular telephone system available to Albanians until then?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Communication with mobile phones was interrupted for Kosova. This happened mainly after the beginning of the NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As well as the fixed telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 24th of March, the beginning of the bombing, did several prominent Albanians lose their lives? If so, can you name those who did?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: After the NATO bombing, that night, the late Bajram Kelmendi was killed with his two sons. He was arrested in his own home, and he was liquidated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were others killed? You've listed them in your --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. The wisest and most outstanding people promoting peaceful movements were killed; Latif Berisha, Agim Hajrizi from Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the effect of those deaths on --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The aim of the deaths or murders was to strike terror among the population by killing those wise men, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 32. Did there come a time shortly after the bombing started when Serb MUP turned up at Dr. Rugova's house? And I think you let them in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Rugova was upstairs and you stayed downstairs, so what you'll tell us will be new. Don't take long over it, but just tell us what happened to you and what did you hear these Serb MUP people saying?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The neighbourhood where Mr. Rugova lived was called Velania, and after the neighbourhood was purged of its inhabitants, the turn came for Rugova's house. An armoured unit came. The number of the police and soldiers was somewhat around ten, I think. They broke down the doors of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. his courtyard and the door of his home. I came down of the upper floor and I told them that there are people here, and then I raised my hands up in the air. I was maltreated by them. And when I told them that this is the house of Mr. Rugova, they said that, "We are doing your job, and this is the man who has been the first to ask for NATO bombing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long were you kept there by these people?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: On the ground floor I was mistreated, as I said, beaten for about an hour, and then they ordered me to call the entire family that was upstairs, which were Mr. Rugova and his family, two of his cousins with their families, myself, my wife. We all went down and for four hours we were detained there without water, without bread, without allowing us to go even to see to our natural needs. And there were even young children, a baby of six months old. A policeman --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a little about this. I think -- were you subsequently instructed as to what you were to do next?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Later that day, did somebody else arrive and instruct Dr. Rugova what he was to do next?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. Later - it was about four hours later - a police official came, and I asked him what was his name. He said, "Jankovic from Suva Reka."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short because we've heard about this. You can give the detail, if necessary, but the upshot of it all was that on the following day, the 1st of April, in accordance with what you were told to do, you left, under police escort, for the White Palace in order to see the accused; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Then at the White Palace, because we can get straight there, the Judges don't need to hear the same account twice, save in respect of important matters. At the White Palace, the beginning of the encounter with the accused, I think you were out of the room and you were with the accused's chef de cabinet, Goran Milenovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you join the meeting? Top of page 9.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I joined the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: -- during the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what passed between you and the accused, if anything.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was invited by Mr. Rugova to be present at that meeting, and he asked me about a press release that the accused asked him to sign. I said that the press releases usually are not signed. Usually they are not signed. And then I communicated with the accused and raised my concern over the dismissal, over the expulsion of the Albanians from Kosova, which at that time was about 700.000, and that -- I told him this is something which must threaten him too. I told him of my concern over the liquidation - at least this is what they were said to be - of some collaborators of Mr. Rugova - Hajrizi, Kelmendi - and the accused ironically took a pencil and wrote the names on a packet of cigarettes and said that, "I will see how to find out what has happened to them." And then when we were discussing why Albanians were leaving Kosova, I said that there are two arguments we have to focus on; why Albanians -- we have to find out why Albanians are leaving Kosova and going to Montenegro when bombing is going on there, and why not a single Serb from the northern part is leaving Serbia when they are, too, afraid of NATO like us but still not leaving their place. These were two arguments which I presented to him while he was claiming that Albanians were leaving Kosova because of NATO and not because of, in fact, his police and military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you refer to the north part, you're referring to Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at that time, was bombing being suffered by those in Vojvodina as it was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The bombing was throughout the territory of Montenegro, Serbia, and Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yet were any of the inhabitants of Vojvodina fleeing in the way that they were fleeing from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: There was not a single case that I have heard of. And I have never heard of any citizen, apart from the Albanians, leaving Kosova. The Albanians left Kosova because of the repression and the special kind of warfare and the expulsion of the Albanians, house by house, giving them five minutes' time to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the meeting at which you were present include some reference to further progress by way of agreement, possibly by way of an interim agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The accused attempted to use Mr. Rugova at this meeting as -- for some kind of political propaganda, but at this meeting too, Mr. Rugova said that a third party is vital and this -- and after Rugova's political liquidation, his physical liquidation would not be an important matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but whether for purposes of political propaganda or otherwise, was something said by the accused about an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 35, for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is this press statement that is under discussion now, that Rugova said that a peaceful path was necessary, and our main part on this side was our permission to leave Kosova. I personally asked for a mechanism so that -- we were being kept as hostages this day, and I asked for our release and asked for telephone connections, and the accused agreed to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that meeting came to an end. There was the question of the press release. Was one issued?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This press release, I am not a witness to its publication because at this time, we didn't get the media at home - our satellite antenna was cut off on the first night - but I heard that it was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, the 2nd of April, where were you, back in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: We returned on the same day, that's 1st of April. And on the next day, the landline telephone was working, and the first call I made, under arrest, was to call Ambassador Hill in Skopje and tell him about what had happened and about the way the police and army had entered the house and about our journey to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, incidentally, have a phone call with the chef de cabinet, Milenovic, on that day?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: On at that day, yes. We had calls from the chef de cabinet of the accused who offered or, rather, insisted that we should meet Ratko Markovic. But we said that these meetings are fruitless because there is no political process under way here, and what is happening is a battle for life or death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did Milenovic say would have been the purpose of your meeting Ratko Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The accused, his chef de cabinet, said, "You should meet to talk about various issues which might have been a continuation of the meeting with the accused on the previous day." But as I said, I was a person who, in our communications, refused very determinedly to meet Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on a couple of days. Were you at Dr. Rugova's house when you received a visit from Nikola Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this the first time you'd met that man or had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It was the first time that this person had come to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that day then, the 4th of April, was it -- I'm putting the date to you, I should have asked you for it. Do you remember if the 4th was the right date or was it some other date?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. What was the purpose of his meeting on that day?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: He came, no doubt on orders of the accused, in order to continue the previous meeting and to issue a press statement for the public and to create the illusion that there was some kind of "political process," in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any sort of statement issued - just yes or no - that day?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next day, did anything happen? Did you have any meetings on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, they brought the Russian ambassador and a meeting was held, and it -- one might say the topic was an implicit one. Our demand was for our release, and we asked the Russian ambassador to use his influence on the accused to secure our release. This meeting was also followed by the media brought by the regime, and at a meeting with journalists, the -- it was arranged for the journalist of Der Spiegel, who was in the house for us -- with us, was sent away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say "they." Who headed this visit?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This meeting was organised by people I mentioned earlier, and the meeting was between Mr. Rugova and the Russian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the people you mentioned earlier. Who in particular turned up on this occasion from the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If one might speak politically, it was led -- led by the accused Sainovic. It was mainly him. And a person who was appointed by the state security, Ljuba Joksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, as to Sainovic on this occasion, did he appear to have authority to act or did he appear to need to refer back to any other superior authority?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I consider that this person was entirely delegated and commanded by the accused and was unable to decide anything off his own bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on what do you base that? Was there anything said or done?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Because at every possible meeting, I told him, "You are the deputy president of the Yugoslav government, and you could take a decision for my release," but he was never able to give me an answer to this question. Then he would disappear for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever say where, other than in him, authority lay? Did he ever say to whom he had to refer?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, he said -- he said that after a day or two, a decision will be made and I will communicate it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When -- that was the 5th of April. When did you next see Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I met Sainovic at intervals. I don't remember the date now. But there was also the meeting with the accused Milutinovic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when was that roughly and by whom was that organised?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This meeting was organised on the insistence of others, without our -- without our consent. It was organised by Sainovic and someone from the state security by phone and with the help of repeated visits. But our response was that we are not ready for these meetings, but we were subjected to pressure with all kinds of strange scenarios at night, firing through the windows and the balconies at night, and this was a way of putting pressure on us to agree to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us the date of the Milutinovic meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was on the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that the only meeting that you had with Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the only meeting you had with Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. There was the first meeting in Belgrade, and the second meeting was in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first meeting in Belgrade, when was that? Can you give the date of that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see you're looking at something; I didn't appreciate that. What are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Excuse me. The second was on the 28th. The first must have been around the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the first meeting, what was Milutinovic's attitude towards you? What did he want? What did he want to tell you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this meeting in Belgrade, the discussion concentrated on -- on rather trivial issues, because it was -- it was generally understood that this so-called political process would yield no results.
