And we were asking every day for -- to be released, and they said that because Rugova does not have any close collaborators nearby, we will allow Merovci to go to Skopje to communicate with colleagues of Rugova there, because there were no normal conditions for work. And we responded rather unfavourably to this proposal at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just taking this first meeting then very shortly, one last or two last points. Was anything said by you or by Milutinovic at that meeting -- I beg your pardon. Was anything said by either you or by Sainovic at that meeting or about the time of that meeting about your status as arrested or detained people?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I could illustrate this with some evidence. At this time, that is the second meeting at Prishtina, I came up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: -- what I might paraphrase was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. Just go back to the question. Did Sainovic say anything about whether you were arrested or not or your status or anything about talking about it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: He didn't talk about our status, but he often said that we were free, but we insisted that he should act on what he said, and we asked that there should be no incidents during the evenings which so frightened the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to move on. Were you able, at some date, to travel to Skopje under police escort?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in Skopje, who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I went to Skopje against my own will, but I went there, and first of all I met all the diplomats, the foreign diplomats, Ambassador Hill, Ambassador Huntzinger. I met Ambassador Walker, Ambassador Petritsch. I also met Mr. Herald Koch, the Assistant Secretary of State for human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think you returned to Kosovo, and you had your second meeting with Milutinovic later in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I returned on the 21st, after two or three days, and I was the only Albanian to enter Kosova. And during my stay in Skopje, I also gave quite a lot of interviews, which I have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the question and just deal with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Milutinovic had arrived from Belgrade, I think, for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. On this meeting of 28th of April, this meeting was again organised in Prishtina against our will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there damage to be seen in Pristina at that time, damage to buildings?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this time, Prishtina was a mysterious place, without anybody on the street, only with paramilitary and military police forces. And all the Albanian shops and businesses were broken into and demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Milutinovic say anything about the damage that he could see, and did you tell him anything about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At these meetings, I personally expressed my indignation at what was happening, and I told him this humanitarian catastrophe of the movement of people under the pressure of the police and the military and these acts of destruction are appalling. And I asked for our immediate release and appealed to him as President of Serbia and as a member of the Serbian government, for an immediate decision to release us and to allow us to go in peace. And Milutinovic said that he would bring us a reply within 24 hours. And indeed we did receive a reply after about two days. The answer was that we had to go to Belgrade on this issue and reach an understanding with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move forward from that meeting. In May of 1999, was there a meeting with a man -- arranged by the man Joksic in Belgrade where you met Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: On 4th of March, we met the people you mentioned and the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that occasion, what was said by the accused?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was a very short and formal meeting, and it was mainly communicated to us that we would leave for Italy, but there was a very nasty undertone. Rugova was asked to leave his family, and we didn't allow this, but the next day, Rugova's family was brought and we flew to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you say anything to any of the other parties at this short meeting about Racak?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At one point, the accused Sainovic, during his unpleasant visit to the house, there was the opportunity to talk about various topics, and I told him that, "Your name is being mentioned in -- unfavourably in connection with the Racak massacre, and one day you might be faced with a charge about this." And he said that this is a game being played by Walker. And this got out into the media and was cited as evidence that the -- this person's orders were behind the Racak massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of other details covered in paragraph 44 of the summary. Before the 24th of March when the bombing started, were different signs put on houses of one kind or another?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases in which apartments were occupied. These were Albanian apartments in which Serbs and policemen and soldiers were housed. And this was a time when every Serb able to bear arms was mobilised, and there was not a single Serbian Kosovan in Prishtina who wasn't mobilised, and these were put into Albanian apartments with signs outside saying, "This is a MUP apartment." As evidence of this, I can say that there were cases in which Albanian families who were unable to -- unable to move used this trick to save themselves from the expeditions of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there rumours circulating at the time about what had happened to Dr. Rugova, rumours that weren't necessarily true?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, there were rumours a little while earlier that Rugova was killed before his house was occupied. As you know, it was mentioned, even when Mr. Rugova testified, a very bad pamphlet circulated as if it was allegedly signed by him. And I would say that before this pamphlet appeared and circulated, Mr. Rugova issued a press release along with -- to the Der Spiegel journalist, and she has got the recorded interview whereby he appealed to the Albanians not to leave Kosova. And this refutes the content of this pamphlet that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask of this witness. And, Your Honour, I'll be grateful for one minute to explain the outstanding issue in relation to the previous witness before the end of the morning. So it will only take a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Do you want to start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have another seven minutes, I don't want to have those seven minutes wasted. I assume you would count them into my time anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin chronologically to review this statement, my first question would be one that is linked to the text of the notes on the talk with Adnan Merovci in Rome, which was disclosed to me by the opposing party under number 03014582. In the Serbian translation, on page 3, there's only one sentence which I would like to quote. Before that, in the paragraph prior to that, it is said that in Pristina, they reviewed the question of departure as if they had been told that they with leave, that the families would go separately so as not to be treated as refugees, and other explanations which apparently they were given in Pristina, and then we have the following sentence: "At the last meeting with Milosevic, Merovci raised this question in Milosevic's presence, saying that the families should go with him and Dr. Rugova, and Milosevic responded that that was okay." So, Mr. Merovci, is this what happened?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is stated in what I was given from -- by the Prosecution as notes on the meeting in Rome. Notes of conversation with Mr. Adnan Merovci in Rome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It didn't matter whether the notes were given by the Prosecution or not. The witness denies that that was what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell me, then, what was the subject of the conversation when you came to see me in Belgrade if it was not Rugova's and your departure? What was the subject of discussion if not that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As I -- I said it earlier in my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you. So let me be more specific. At that last meeting, was anything else discussed but Rugova's departure together with his family and also your own from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I said earlier we discussed nothing else than the attempt to separate Rugova and myself from our respective families and that we reacted to that firmly. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. Let us make things quite clear. Was anything else discussed at that meeting except your request to leave Kosovo where you felt you were threatened?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: We had -- we had requested earlier, and we heard from Milutinovic that we had to go to Belgrade to discuss this issue with you. We came and what happened that I said earlier happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was anything else discussed? Was there a discussion about anything other topic? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you came only to discuss that you or, rather, Rugova and you, someone accompanying him, should leave Kosovo and Metohija because you didn't feel safe there. That was the only topic of discussion, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that. Now, rather than go on again, we'll adjourn now. It's coming up to time. Mr. Merovci, could you bear in mind, please, during the adjournment -- would you be back at 9.00 tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence, and would you bear in mind during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the previous witness and His Honour Judge Kwon's question? The position is that protective measures were requested on the 14th of November on the grounds of safety and security of the witness, and I think, though I haven't been able to track everything down, I think this would be on the basis of perceived risk arising from his contact with particular individuals, some of whom have been named in his evidence. Following the grant of those protective measures and a request by the Chamber that we should be more specific or should be specific in our seeking protective measures, my recollection is that all witnesses were contacted again, and that led to the motion of the 15th of March, having in its first footnote an observation to the effect that this witness and one other would not be requiring protective measures and would be giving evidence in open session. So it was sought out of an abundance of caution, and the witness was right that he had not sought them himself personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
